script.opening: "Doctor, I can’t stay awake in the day — I fall asleep without warning, even mid-conversation or in lectures, however much I sleep at night. And this strange thing happens: when I laugh hard or get a fright, my knees buckle and my face goes slack for a few seconds. I also get terrifying moments where I can’t move as I’m falling asleep. People think I’m just lazy. It’s wrecking my studies."

facts.text: Since about age 17, worse in the last year. Falls asleep in lectures, on the bus, once mid-conversation with a friend, once while eating. A short nap of 15–20 minutes refreshes her, then it creeps back. "Not really tired — it just comes over me."

When she laughs hard or is startled, her knees go weak, her jaw drops and her head nods for a few seconds. Fully aware throughout — "I can hear everything, I just can’t hold myself up". Has never fallen to the ground fully; grabs a chair. Laughing sets it off most.

In bed 11pm to 8am but wakes many times. Sometimes wakes unable to move for a minute, and sees a figure in the room that isn’t there — "terrifying". Vivid dreams. Doesn’t snore that anyone has said; flatmate hasn’t noticed pauses in breathing.

No shift work. Not using sleeping pills or recreational drugs; cannabis twice at university, not for a year. Alcohol: a few drinks at weekends. Coffee 3–4 a day to stay awake. BMI 22. No heavy periods, not tired from anaemia that she knows of. No thyroid symptoms. No head injury.
"Low sometimes, because I’m falling behind and people think I don’t care." Enjoys things, sleeping isn’t the problem, appetite fine. No thoughts of self-harm.
Has a driving licence and drives her mum’s car home at weekends (an hour on the motorway). Has "nodded off at traffic lights once". Cooks on a gas hob in her student flat.
Third-year history student; has failed two essays and been told she may not progress. No medicines except the combined pill. No allergies. No family history of sleep problems.

Articulate, embarrassed, worried you will be called lazy again. If the doctor explains it may be a real neurological condition, show relief: "So it’s a real thing? Not me?" Be upset but accepting about not driving if it is explained kindly. Admit the near-miss at the traffic lights only if driving is asked about.

ice.ideas: "I honestly don’t know. I started to wonder if they’re right and I’m just lazy."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — failing her course; and the frightening episodes. Privately she wonders if the knee-buckling is a kind of epilepsy.
ice.expectations: "Find out what it is, and get some help — maybe a letter for the university."

cues: "People think I’m just lazy" — she needs to be believed.
"My knees buckle when I laugh" — cataplexy, the specific clue.
"I drive home at weekends" (if asked) — driving safety and DVLA advice.

checkpoints.text: Recognises NARCOLEPSY — chronic excessive daytime sleepiness with irresistible sleep attacks plus REM-intrusion phenomena (sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations)
Recognises CATAPLEXY (emotion/laughter-triggered transient loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness) as highly specific for narcolepsy type 1

Excludes other causes of excessive daytime sleepiness (insufficient/poor sleep, OSA, depression, drugs/alcohol, shift work, other hypersomnias; syncope/seizure for the spells) and uses an Epworth-type assessment
Does NOT mislabel the patient as lazy/depressed, takes the symptoms seriously, and validates the impact

REFERS to sleep/neurology for diagnosis (polysomnography/MSLT ± orexin) and treatment (scheduled naps/sleep hygiene, modafinil/stimulants — specialist-initiated, with the MHRA November 2020 pregnancy and contraception warning for modafinil — cataplexy agents), and addresses DVLA/DRIVING (must stop and notify)
Validates the distress and the "lazy" mislabelling, explains the likely diagnosis sensitively, and checks understanding
Addresses the educational/psychosocial impact and the driving issue supportively
Safety-nets and follows up: sleep/neurology referral, driving/safety advice, impact support, and review — recognising the sleepiness+cataplexy pattern and referring, not dismissing as laziness

worked.txt: "You are NOT lazy — what you’re describing sounds like a real neurological sleep condition called narcolepsy. The uncontrollable daytime sleep attacks, the paralysis as you fall asleep, and especially your knees buckling when you laugh all fit."
"That last one — losing muscle strength with strong emotion while staying fully aware — is called cataplexy, and it’s quite specific for narcolepsy. It’s not fainting or a fit."

"Let me check a few things — how much sleep you actually get, any snoring or gasping at night, your mood, and any medications. I’ll use a quick sleepiness score, the Epworth scale, and a two-week sleep diary too."

"I’m referring you to the sleep/neurology specialists, who confirm it with sleep studies and can treat it — things like scheduled short naps, a wake-promoting medicine for the sleepiness, and treatment for the cataplexy. If they suggest modafinil, it can harm a baby in pregnancy and stops the pill and other hormonal contraception working as well, so we’d talk about reliable contraception. It’s manageable."

"One important thing: this kind of sleepiness affects driving — you must stop driving now and tell the DVLA. You can reapply once the specialist confirms your symptoms have been well controlled for at least 3 months. We’ll go through that and how you’ll get around."
"This has clearly hit your studies and confidence — we can support that, including letting your university know it’s a medical condition. Come back if things worsen, and I’ll chase the referral."

f.learning: NARCOLEPSY is chronic EXCESSIVE DAYTIME SLEEPINESS with irresistible SLEEP attacks (falling asleep mid-activity, unrefreshing despite adequate night sleep) plus REM-intrusion phenomena — SLEEP PARALYSIS, HYPNAGOGIC/hypnopompic HALLUCINATIONS and fragmented night sleep. The highly specific clue is CATAPLEXY — sudden, transient loss of muscle tone (knees buckling, head drooping, facial slackening) triggered by strong EMOTION, classically LAUGHTER, with PRESERVED consciousness (distinguishing it from syncope/seizure) — which characterises narcolepsy type 1 (orexin/hypocretin deficiency). Distinguish narcolepsy from other causes of excessive daytime sleepiness: insufficient/poor sleep, obstructive sleep apnoea (snoring/witnessed apnoeas/obesity), depression, drugs/alcohol, shift work and other hypersomnias, using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (above 10 suggests excessive sleepiness) and a two-week sleep diary. Patients are frequently mislabelled as lazy or depressed and endure years of diagnostic delay, so take the symptoms seriously and validate the impact on studies, mood and relationships rather than dismissing them. Refer to a sleep/neurology service for diagnosis (polysomnography and Multiple Sleep Latency Test, ± CSF orexin) and treatment — sleep hygiene with scheduled naps, wake-promoting agents (e.g. modafinil, specialist-initiated; it can harm an unborn baby and reduces the effect of hormonal contraception, so effective contraception is needed, MHRA Drug Safety Update November 2020; solriamfetol per NICE TA758) for sleepiness, and specific agents for cataplexy — and address the DVLA/DRIVING implications (under current DVLA standards a Group 1 driver with narcolepsy must stop driving and notify the DVLA, with relicensing considered after satisfactory symptom control for at least 3 months confirmed by the specialist; Group 2 is much stricter) and the psychosocial/educational impact (Equality Act 2010 reasonable adjustments; mood). The skill is recognising the sleepiness + cataplexy + REM-phenomena pattern, not mislabelling it laziness/depression, and referring appropriately.

knowledge.guideline: [1] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current online version), section on primary/central hypersomnias including narcolepsy · [2] NICE TA758 (solriamfetol for excessive daytime sleepiness caused by narcolepsy, 2022) · [3] MHRA Drug Safety Update (November 2020): modafinil and the risk of congenital malformations · [4] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA (2017) · [5] Equality Act 2010
knowledge.summary: Irresistible daytime sleep attacks with cataplexy (brief loss of muscle tone set off by laughter or surprise, with full awareness), sleep paralysis and vivid hallucinations at sleep onset make narcolepsy type 1 the working diagnosis. The GP’s job is to recognise the pattern, rule out common causes of sleepiness, measure sleepiness with the Epworth scale, refer to a specialist sleep service, and deal with driving and safety on the day. Treatment is specialist-led. A person with narcolepsy must stop driving and tell the DVLA.

points.t: Persistent excessive daytime sleepiness with sleep attacks that feel irresistible, often with short naps that refresh for a while. Look for REM-intrusion features: sleep paralysis, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations and broken night sleep. Onset is usually in the teens or twenties, and diagnosis is often delayed by years.

Sudden, brief weakness set off by strong emotion, usually laughter: knees buckling, jaw or face going slack, head dropping. The person stays fully aware and remembers the episode. That separates it from syncope and seizures. Cataplexy points to narcolepsy type 1 (orexin deficiency).

Too little or irregular sleep, obstructive sleep apnoea (snoring, witnessed apnoeas, raised BMI), depression, alcohol, cannabis and other drugs, sedating medicines, shift work, and medical causes such as hypothyroidism or anaemia. A two-week sleep diary and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (a score above 10 suggests excessive sleepiness) are useful before referral.

Diagnosis needs a specialist sleep or neurology service: overnight polysomnography followed by a Multiple Sleep Latency Test, sometimes CSF orexin. Refer when narcolepsy is suspected; do not start wake-promoting drugs in primary care before the diagnosis.

Regular sleep times and short planned naps. Modafinil is the usual first drug for sleepiness (BNF). It can harm an unborn baby and it lowers the effect of hormonal contraception, so effective contraception is needed (MHRA [3]). Solriamfetol is an option if modafinil and dexamfetamine or methylphenidate have not worked well enough or are not suitable (NICE TA758 [2]). Cataplexy has its own treatments, chosen by the specialist.

Under current DVLA standards for primary/central hypersomnias, including narcolepsy, a Group 1 driver must stop driving and tell the DVLA. Relicensing is considered only after satisfactory symptom control, for at least 3 months, confirmed by the specialist. Group 2 (lorry and bus) licensing is much stricter and needs specialist assessment [1]. If she keeps driving against advice, the GMC allows the doctor to tell the DVLA after telling her first [4].

Narcolepsy is likely to count as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 [5], so her university must consider reasonable adjustments (extra time, rest breaks, recorded lectures). Screen for low mood, which is common. Give safety advice about cooking, bathing, swimming and heights while cataplexy is untreated.

model.text: Hello Orla, I’m Dr Patel. What’s brought you in today?

I can’t stay awake in the day. I fall asleep without warning, even in the middle of a conversation or in lectures, however much I sleep at night. And when I laugh hard or get a fright, my knees buckle and my face goes slack for a few seconds. People think I’m just lazy. It’s wrecking my studies.
That sounds exhausting, and hard to live with when people misjudge you. I’d like to hear more about the sleepiness and those episodes, then I’ll explain what I think is going on. Is that okay?
model.why: Acknowledges the impact and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes, please.
When you fall asleep in the day, what is it like? Can you fight it?
Not really. It just comes over me. I might nap for a bit and feel better, then it comes back.
Tell me about the knees buckling. When it happens, are you aware of what’s going on around you?
model.why: Checks for preserved awareness to separate cataplexy from syncope or seizure

model.text: Yes, completely. I can hear everything, I just can’t hold myself up for a few seconds. Laughing sets it off most.
Have you ever bitten your tongue, wet yourself, or been confused afterwards?
No, never.
You mentioned something happens as you fall asleep. Can you tell me about that?
model.why: Follows the cue about night-time symptoms

model.text: I wake up and can’t move, and sometimes I see things in the room that aren’t there. It’s terrifying.
That must be frightening. What time do you usually go to bed and get up, and how is your sleep at night?
I go to bed at a normal time and I’m in bed long enough, but I wake up a lot.
Has anyone said you snore loudly or stop breathing in your sleep?
Not that anyone’s said.
Some other things can cause sleepiness, so I ask everyone. How much alcohol, caffeine or cannabis do you use, and do you take any medicines, including anything bought over the counter?
Nothing much, no.
And how has your mood been through all this?
Low sometimes, because I’m falling behind and people think I don’t care. But I’m not depressed like that. I want to get on with things.
Have you ever had thoughts of harming yourself?
No, nothing like that.
What have you been thinking might be going on?
I honestly don’t know. I started to wonder if they’re right and I’m lazy.
You’re not lazy. What you describe is something real. What worries you most about it?
Failing my course. And the episodes. I don’t know what they are.
And what were you hoping I could do today?
Find out what it is, and get some help.

I think this is probably a condition called narcolepsy. It’s a problem with how the brain controls sleep and wakefulness. The sleep attacks, being unable to move as you fall asleep, and seeing things at that time all fit. The knee-buckling when you laugh, while you stay fully aware, has a name, cataplexy. It’s quite specific for narcolepsy, and it isn’t fainting or a fit.
model.why: Names the likely diagnosis and explains cataplexy

model.text: So it’s a real thing? Not me?

It’s a real neurological condition, and it’s treatable. I’m going to ask you to fill in a short sleepiness score now, and keep a sleep diary for two weeks. I’ll also check some bloods to rule out things like thyroid problems or anaemia that can add to tiredness.
model.why: Epworth score, sleep diary and bloods for contributors

model.text: Okay.

The diagnosis is confirmed by a specialist sleep service with an overnight sleep study and a daytime nap test. I’ll refer you. Treatment usually means regular sleep times, short planned naps, and medicine for the sleepiness and for the cataplexy, all started by the specialist.
model.why: Specialist referral and outline of treatment

model.text: That’s a relief, honestly.
There’s one important thing I have to raise. Do you drive?
I do, yes.

With sleep attacks like these, driving isn’t safe at the moment. The DVLA rules say you must stop driving now and tell them yourself. Once the specialist has your symptoms well controlled for at least three months, you can apply to have your licence back.
model.why: Clear DVLA advice using current standards

model.text: Stop completely? I need the car to get around.
I know that’s a big thing to hear, and I’m sorry. Falling asleep at the wheel could kill you or someone else. Could we look at other ways to get to university while this is sorted out?
model.why: Acknowledges the loss while staying clear on safety

model.text: I suppose I can get the bus. I didn’t realise.

Until the cataplexy is treated, take care with things like hot pans, baths, swimming and heights, because you could drop suddenly. And your university should offer support, such as extra time or recorded lectures. I can write a letter confirming this is a medical condition.
model.why: Practical safety advice and educational support

model.text: That would really help.

If your mood drops a lot, or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, come back straight away. Come back too if the episodes change, for example if you lose awareness, or if you haven’t heard about the referral in a few weeks. Can you tell me what you’ll do from today?
Stop driving and tell the DVLA. Do the sleep diary and bloods. Wait for the sleep clinic. Be careful in the bath and kitchen. Come back if my mood gets bad.
Exactly right. Let’s book a review in two to three weeks to go through the diary and bloods.

social.t: Falling behind and being judged hurts self-esteem. A letter confirming a medical condition helps her ask the university for adjustments and, where eligible, Disabled Students’ Allowance support.
Losing the car affects independence. Plan other ways to travel before she leaves the room.

legal.t: Current DVLA standards for narcolepsy: Group 1 drivers must stop driving and notify the DVLA; relicensing is considered after satisfactory symptom control for at least 3 months, confirmed by the specialist. Group 2 licensing needs specialist assessment and is much stricter.
Narcolepsy is likely to meet the definition of disability, so education providers and employers must consider reasonable adjustments.

professional.t: Record the driving advice. If she keeps driving against advice, GMC guidance (Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive, 2017) allows the doctor to tell the DVLA, after telling her first.
Wake-promoting medicines are specialist-initiated. If modafinil is started, check contraception and pregnancy plans (MHRA Drug Safety Update, November 2020; BNF).

community.t: Narcolepsy UK offers patient information, including on driving and education.

redFlags: Sleep attacks while driving or operating machinery
Loss of awareness, tongue biting, incontinence or confusion after episodes: think seizure
Loud snoring or witnessed apnoeas: OSA
ice: Concern: failing her course; the unexplained episodes

playbook.diagnosis: Suspected narcolepsy type 1: excessive daytime sleepiness with sleep attacks, cataplexy with preserved awareness, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations. Needs specialist confirmation after exclusion of insufficient sleep, OSA, depression and substance effects.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “I think you have narcolepsy. It’s a condition where the brain doesn’t control sleep and wakefulness properly. It explains the sleep attacks, the paralysis at night and your knees giving way when you laugh. It’s real, it isn’t laziness, and it can be treated.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in half-believing people who say you’re lazy. What you’ve told me points to a real neurological condition, and we’ll get it properly diagnosed.”
management.psychosocial: University letter and adjustments; travel plans without the car; mood support.

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating a neurological illness as a lifestyle problem, and by forgetting the car keys in her pocket.

items.fail: Calling it poor sleep habits or depression.
items.why: Sleep attacks with cataplexy and REM-intrusion features are narcolepsy until proven otherwise.
items.fix: Ask about cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hallucinations in every sleepy young adult.

items.why: Sleep attacks at the wheel can be fatal, and the DVLA requires her to stop and notify.
items.fix: Ask ‘Do you drive?’ and give clear, current DVLA advice.

items.fail: Mistaking cataplexy for fainting or seizures.
items.why: Preserved awareness with an emotional trigger is the key feature.
items.fix: Ask whether she is aware during episodes and what sets them off.

items.why: Diagnosis needs specialist tests; modafinil carries pregnancy and contraception risks.
items.fix: Refer to a sleep service and leave medicines to the specialist.

items.why: It is the hurt she brought, and lifting it builds trust.
items.fix: Say clearly that this is a real condition, not laziness.

items.why: Untreated cataplexy risks injury, and mood often suffers.
items.fix: Give home safety advice, a mood safety net and a review date.

wordPics.fail: Tells her to sleep more and cut out caffeine, or labels it depression; misses cataplexy; never asks about driving; no referral.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the sleepiness and cataplexy pattern, excludes common causes, refers to a sleep service, and advises her to stop driving and tell the DVLA.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: explicitly lifts the ‘lazy’ label; explains cataplexy clearly; handles the driving news with empathy and practical alternatives; gives safety advice and university support; screens mood and risk; clear teach-back and follow-up.

avoid.dont: “You probably just need a better sleep routine.”
avoid.instead: “You’re not lazy. This sounds like narcolepsy, a real neurological condition, and I’m referring you to find out.”
avoid.why: Years of dismissal are the usual story; recognising the pattern is the key task.

avoid.dont: “Maybe cut down on driving for a bit.”
avoid.instead: “You must stop driving now and tell the DVLA. You can reapply once the specialist has your symptoms controlled.”
avoid.why: The DVLA standard is to stop, not to cut down. Vague advice is unsafe.

avoid.dont: “I’ll start you on modafinil to see if it helps.”
avoid.instead: “The sleep specialist will confirm it and start the right treatment.”
avoid.why: Diagnosis needs specialist testing, and modafinil carries pregnancy and contraception risks (MHRA, November 2020).

I know that’s a big thing to hear, and I’m sorry. Falling asleep at the wheel could kill you or someone else. Could we look at other ways to get to university while this is sorted out?
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges the loss while staying clear on safety

SCA_MODELS.text: I suppose I can get the bus. I didn’t realise.

Until the cataplexy is treated, take care with things like hot pans, baths, swimming and heights, because you could drop suddenly. And your university should offer support, such as extra time or recorded lectures. I can write a letter confirming this is a medical condition.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical safety advice and educational support

SCA_MODELS.text: That would really help.

If your mood drops a lot, or you have any thoughts of harming yourself, come back straight away. Come back too if the episodes change, for example if you lose awareness, or if you haven’t heard about the referral in a few weeks. Can you tell me what you’ll do from today?
Stop driving and tell the DVLA. Do the sleep diary and bloods. Wait for the sleep clinic. Be careful in the bath and kitchen. Come back if my mood gets bad.
Exactly right. Let’s book a review in two to three weeks to go through the diary and bloods.

SCA_STEM.name: Orla Hennessy
SCA_STEM.recent: Months to years of overwhelming daytime sleepiness with sudden sleep attacks, even mid-conversation and in lectures. Brief episodes of her knees buckling and face going slack when she laughs or is startled. Frightening episodes of being unable to move as she falls asleep. Studies and mood affected.
SCA_STEM.reason: “I can’t stay awake in the day, and people think I’m just lazy.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current online version), section on primary/central hypersomnias including narcolepsy · [2] NICE TA758 (solriamfetol for excessive daytime sleepiness caused by narcolepsy, 2022) · [3] MHRA Drug Safety Update (November 2020): modafinil and the risk of congenital malformations · [4] GMC Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive and reporting concerns to the DVLA (2017) · [5] Equality Act 2010
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Irresistible daytime sleep attacks with cataplexy (brief loss of muscle tone set off by laughter or surprise, with full awareness), sleep paralysis and vivid hallucinations at sleep onset make narcolepsy type 1 the working diagnosis. The GP’s job is to recognise the pattern, rule out common causes of sleepiness, measure sleepiness with the Epworth scale, refer to a specialist sleep service, and deal with driving and safety on the day. Treatment is specialist-led. A person with narcolepsy must stop driving and tell the DVLA.

points.t: Persistent excessive daytime sleepiness with sleep attacks that feel irresistible, often with short naps that refresh for a while. Look for REM-intrusion features: sleep paralysis, hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations and broken night sleep. Onset is usually in the teens or twenties, and diagnosis is often delayed by years.

Sudden, brief weakness set off by strong emotion, usually laughter: knees buckling, jaw or face going slack, head dropping. The person stays fully aware and remembers the episode. That separates it from syncope and seizures. Cataplexy points to narcolepsy type 1 (orexin deficiency).

Too little or irregular sleep, obstructive sleep apnoea (snoring, witnessed apnoeas, raised BMI), depression, alcohol, cannabis and other drugs, sedating medicines, shift work, and medical causes such as hypothyroidism or anaemia. A two-week sleep diary and the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (a score above 10 suggests excessive sleepiness) are useful before referral.

Diagnosis needs a specialist sleep or neurology service: overnight polysomnography followed by a Multiple Sleep Latency Test, sometimes CSF orexin. Refer when narcolepsy is suspected; do not start wake-promoting drugs in primary care before the diagnosis.

Regular sleep times and short planned naps. Modafinil is the usual first drug for sleepiness (BNF). It can harm an unborn baby and it lowers the effect of hormonal contraception, so effective contraception is needed (MHRA [3]). Solriamfetol is an option if modafinil and dexamfetamine or methylphenidate have not worked well enough or are not suitable (NICE TA758 [2]). Cataplexy has its own treatments, chosen by the specialist.

Under current DVLA standards for primary/central hypersomnias, including narcolepsy, a Group 1 driver must stop driving and tell the DVLA. Relicensing is considered only after satisfactory symptom control, for at least 3 months, confirmed by the specialist. Group 2 (lorry and bus) licensing is much stricter and needs specialist assessment [1]. If she keeps driving against advice, the GMC allows the doctor to tell the DVLA after telling her first [4].

Narcolepsy is likely to count as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 [5], so her university must consider reasonable adjustments (extra time, rest breaks, recorded lectures). Screen for low mood, which is common. Give safety advice about cooking, bathing, swimming and heights while cataplexy is untreated.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her describe the sleep attacks, the knee-buckling and the night-time episodes before narrowing.
Explored the effect on her studies, mood and self-image, and whether she drives.
Picked up the emotion-triggered weakness with preserved awareness as cataplexy, and the ‘lazy’ label as a source of distress.
Idea: maybe she is lazy. Concern: failing her course and the unexplained episodes. Expectation: a diagnosis and help.
Epworth Sleepiness Scale, two-week sleep diary, and bloods (FBC, TFT and others) for contributors; no specialist tests in primary care.
Narcolepsy type 1 versus insufficient sleep, OSA, depression, drugs, other hypersomnias; cataplexy versus syncope and seizure.
Checked seizure features, snoring and apnoeas, substances and medicines, and screened mood and self-harm risk.
Suspected narcolepsy with cataplexy (type 1), pending specialist confirmation.
Referral to a specialist sleep service; sleep routine and planned naps explained; medicines left to the specialist; safety advice while cataplexy is untreated.
Stop driving and tell the DVLA now; university letter and reasonable adjustments; mood support.
Return for low mood, self-harm thoughts or changed episodes; chase the referral if no news; review in 2–3 weeks with the diary and bloods.

social.t: Falling behind and being judged hurts self-esteem. A letter confirming a medical condition helps her ask the university for adjustments and, where eligible, Disabled Students’ Allowance support.
Losing the car affects independence. Plan other ways to travel before she leaves the room.

legal.t: Current DVLA standards for narcolepsy: Group 1 drivers must stop driving and notify the DVLA; relicensing is considered after satisfactory symptom control for at least 3 months, confirmed by the specialist. Group 2 licensing needs specialist assessment and is much stricter.
Narcolepsy is likely to meet the definition of disability, so education providers and employers must consider reasonable adjustments.

professional.t: Record the driving advice. If she keeps driving against advice, GMC guidance (Confidentiality: patients’ fitness to drive, 2017) allows the doctor to tell the DVLA, after telling her first.
Wake-promoting medicines are specialist-initiated. If modafinil is started, check contraception and pregnancy plans (MHRA Drug Safety Update, November 2020; BNF).

community.t: Narcolepsy UK offers patient information, including on driving and education.

redFlags: Sleep attacks while driving or operating machinery
Loss of awareness, tongue biting, incontinence or confusion after episodes: think seizure
Loud snoring or witnessed apnoeas: OSA
ice: Concern: failing her course; the unexplained episodes

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Suspected narcolepsy type 1: excessive daytime sleepiness with sleep attacks, cataplexy with preserved awareness, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations. Needs specialist confirmation after exclusion of insufficient sleep, OSA, depression and substance effects.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “I think you have narcolepsy. It’s a condition where the brain doesn’t control sleep and wakefulness properly. It explains the sleep attacks, the paralysis at night and your knees giving way when you laugh. It’s real, it isn’t laziness, and it can be treated.”

management.reflectIce: “You came in half-believing people who say you’re lazy. What you’ve told me points to a real neurological condition, and we’ll get it properly diagnosed.”
management.psychosocial: University letter and adjustments; travel plans without the car; mood support.

Bloods for contributors (FBC, TFT and others as indicated)
Referral to a specialist sleep service for polysomnography and MSLT
Stop driving now and notify the DVLA (current DVLA standards)
Safety advice while cataplexy is untreated; medicines left to the specialist
safetyNet: Return urgently for self-harm thoughts or much lower mood
Return if episodes change, such as loss of awareness
Chase the referral if no appointment within a few weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by treating a neurological illness as a lifestyle problem, and by forgetting the car keys in her pocket.

items.fail: Calling it poor sleep habits or depression.
items.why: Sleep attacks with cataplexy and REM-intrusion features are narcolepsy until proven otherwise.
items.fix: Ask about cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hallucinations in every sleepy young adult.

items.why: Sleep attacks at the wheel can be fatal, and the DVLA requires her to stop and notify.
items.fix: Ask ‘Do you drive?’ and give clear, current DVLA advice.

items.fail: Mistaking cataplexy for fainting or seizures.
items.why: Preserved awareness with an emotional trigger is the key feature.
items.fix: Ask whether she is aware during episodes and what sets them off.

items.why: Diagnosis needs specialist tests; modafinil carries pregnancy and contraception risks.
items.fix: Refer to a sleep service and leave medicines to the specialist.

items.why: It is the hurt she brought, and lifting it builds trust.
items.fix: Say clearly that this is a real condition, not laziness.

items.why: Untreated cataplexy risks injury, and mood often suffers.
items.fix: Give home safety advice, a mood safety net and a review date.
